_notes: Per-zone factual data for V3 Phase 2. DST dates are for current_year 2026 and were checked against IANA tz database behavior. City population figures are city proper or closest official urban/local-government statistic available, rounded to the nearest thousand for display consistency.

geography.description: Eastern North America from the Atlantic seaboard to the eastern Great Lakes, including the US East Coast, eastern Canada, the Bahamas, and parts of the Caribbean.

history.note: Adopted in 1883 with the establishment of standard railroad time zones in North America.

dst.note: Most of Mexico no longer observes DST as of 2022; only a few border-state municipalities still do.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.note: Abolished DST in 2022 except border municipalities

geography.description: Central North America from the Great Plains through Texas and into Mexico and most of Central America.

history.note: Adopted with the 1883 standard railroad time zones; has the largest population of any North American zone due to Mexico's inclusion.

dst.note: Most of Arizona stays on MST year-round (does not observe DST). The Navajo Nation within Arizona does observe DST.

countries.name: United States (mountain)
countries.note: Most of Arizona does not observe DST

geography.description: The North American mountain region from the Canadian Northwest Territories through the Rocky Mountains and into northwestern Mexico.

history.note: Adopted with the 1883 standard railroad time zones. Arizona opted out of DST in 1968 due to its hot summer climate.

countries.name: Canada (British Columbia, Yukon)
countries.note: Yukon stays on PDT year-round (effectively MST)

notable_institutions.name: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

geography.description: West coast of North America from southern Alaska to Baja California, including the major US tech industry hubs.

history.note: Adopted with the 1883 standard railroad time zones.

notable_institutions.name: U.S. Geological Survey Alaska Science Center

geography.description: Most of Alaska except the Aleutian Islands. Covers the largest land area of any US time zone but has the smallest population.

history.note: Alaska was consolidated from four time zones into two (Alaska and Hawaii-Aleutian) in 1983.

dst.note: Hawaii does not observe DST. The Aleutian Islands portion of HAST does observe DST (becoming HADT, UTC−9), but population there is negligible. For practical purposes HST is a fixed-offset zone.

geography.description: The state of Hawaii and the western Aleutian Islands of Alaska. The most westerly time zone in the United States.

history.note: Hawaii originally used UTC−10:30 until 1947, when it shifted to UTC−10. Hawaii has not observed DST since 1933.

dst.note: UTC is the global reference time standard. By definition, it does not observe daylight saving.

countries.name: (Reference standard, not a civil time zone)
countries.note: UTC is not a civil time zone for any country. It is the global reference for civil time, computing systems, aviation, and maritime applications.

notable_institutions.name: International Bureau of Weights and Measures
International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service

geography.description: UTC is a global reference standard, not a geographic zone. It is the basis for all civil time zone offsets worldwide.

history.note: UTC was formally adopted in 1972, replacing GMT as the primary world time standard. It is maintained by atomic clocks and adjusted with leap seconds (though leap seconds are scheduled to be discontinued by 2035).

dst.summer_name: British Summer Time / Western European Summer Time
dst.note: GMT countries vary. The UK, Ireland, and Portugal observe summer time; Iceland and most of West Africa remain on GMT year-round.

military_code.name: Zulu
military_code.note: Shares the Zulu designation with UTC because their offsets are identical.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.note: GMT in winter, BST in summer

principal_cities.name: Casablanca
principal_cities.note: Morocco uses GMT+1 most of year, drops to GMT during Ramadan

geography.description: Western Europe and most of West Africa, anchored at the Prime Meridian at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.

history.note: Established by international agreement at the 1884 International Meridian Conference. GMT was the world time reference until UTC formally replaced it in 1972.

dst.note: EU Summer Time changes happen at the same moment across all EU member states.

geography.description: Most of continental Western and Central Europe, plus parts of North Africa. The most densely populated time zone in Europe.

history.note: Adopted by Germany and Austria-Hungary in 1893; expanded across most of continental Europe through the 20th century.

dst.note: India does not observe daylight saving time. The IST offset of UTC+5:30 is constant year-round. Note: 'IST' is sometimes ambiguous — it can also refer to Irish Standard Time (Ireland's summer time). On TimeAtlas, IST refers exclusively to India Standard Time.

military_code.note: IST has a 30-minute offset and does not have a standard NATO/military code. Some sources use the unofficial designation 'E*' (Echo-star) for half-hour zones, but this is not formally recognized.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
countries.note: Sri Lanka also uses UTC+5:30, though its zone identifier is technically separate

geography.description: All of India and Sri Lanka. India uses a single time zone despite spanning roughly 30° of longitude — a unique choice among large countries.

history.note: IST was established when India gained independence in 1947. India debated dual time zones (one for the east, one for the west) several times but has retained the single-zone system.

dst.note: Japan has not observed daylight saving time since 1951.

geography.description: All of Japan, from Hokkaido in the north to Okinawa in the south.

history.note: JST was established in 1888 based on the meridian at Akashi (135° E). Japan briefly observed DST during the US occupation (1948–1951) but abolished it as unpopular and has not used it since.

dst.note: New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, and the Australian Capital Territory observe DST; Queensland remains on AEST year-round.

countries.name: Australia (eastern states)
countries.note: Queensland does not observe DST, while NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, and ACT do.

geography.description: Eastern Australia, spanning the populous east coast from Queensland through New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, and the Australian Capital Territory.

history.note: Eastern Australian colonies adopted standard time in the 1890s; state-level DST rules later diverged, especially Queensland non-observance.

dst.note: AEDT is the daylight-saving designation used in southeastern Australia; Queensland remains on AEST and is not represented by this daylight code.

geography.description: Southeastern Australia during daylight saving months, covering New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, and the Australian Capital Territory.

history.note: Modern recurring daylight saving in southeastern Australia developed in the early 1970s, with state rules aligned to the current October-April pattern.

dst.note: South Australia observes DST; the Northern Territory remains on ACST year-round.

military_code.note: ACST has a half-hour offset and does not have a standard NATO/military time-zone letter.

countries.name: Australia (central states and territories)
countries.note: South Australia observes DST; Northern Territory does not.

geography.description: Central Australia, covering South Australia and the Northern Territory with a distinctive half-hour offset.

history.note: South Australia adopted a central half-hour standard in the 1890s; the Northern Territory retained the same standard offset without DST.

dst.note: Western Australia does not observe DST; state referendums have repeatedly rejected permanent daylight saving.

notable_institutions.name: Chamber of Minerals and Energy of Western Australia

geography.description: Western Australia, from Perth and the Indian Ocean coast across the sparsely populated interior.

history.note: Western Australia adopted standard time in 1895 and has remained on UTC+8 outside short DST trials.

geography.description: New Zealand mainland and nearby dependencies, one of the earliest major economies to begin each calendar day.

history.note: New Zealand adopted a national standard time in 1868, among the earliest countries to do so.

dst.note: NZDT is the daylight-saving designation for New Zealand during the southern summer.

military_code.note: UTC+13 is outside the standard single-letter NATO/military time-zone range.

geography.description: New Zealand during daylight saving months, operating one hour ahead of NZST across the same national territory.

history.note: New Zealand first experimented with summer time in 1927; the modern NZDT season is defined by national daylight saving legislation.

dst.note: Singapore does not observe DST.

geography.description: The city-state of Singapore at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, using UTC+8 for economic alignment with East Asia.

history.note: Singapore moved to UTC+8 in 1982 to align clocks with Malaysia and major East Asian trading partners.

dst.note: Hong Kong has not observed DST since 1979.

geography.description: Hong Kong on the South China coast, sharing UTC+8 with mainland China while maintaining its own IANA identifier.

history.note: Hong Kong adopted standard time in the early 20th century and discontinued daylight saving after 1979.

dst.note: South Korea does not currently observe DST; temporary DST experiments ended in 1988.

geography.description: The Korean Peninsula, centered near 127°E and aligned with Japan Standard Time at UTC+9.

history.note: South Korea standardized on UTC+9 in 1961; North Korea returned to UTC+9 in 2018 after a brief UTC+8:30 period.

dst.note: Brazil abolished nationwide daylight saving time in 2019.

geography.description: Eastern and central Brazil, including the national capital Brasília and the São Paulo-Rio economic corridor.

history.note: Brazil introduced legal time zones in 1914; Brasília time became the principal national reference for government and markets.

dst.note: Argentina does not currently observe DST.

notable_institutions.name: Banco Central de la República Argentina

geography.description: Argentina from the Río de la Plata through Patagonia, using a single UTC−3 civil time nationwide.

history.note: Argentina formalized national standard time in the early 20th century and has used several historical DST experiments, none currently active.

dst.note: Most of continental Chile observes DST; the Magallanes Region stays on UTC−3 year-round.

countries.name: Chile (continental)
countries.note: Magallanes uses UTC−3 year-round; Easter Island uses a separate offset.

geography.description: Continental Chile, a long north-south Pacific corridor mostly west of the Andes.

history.note: Chile adopted legal standard time in the early 20th century; modern DST rules have changed frequently and are tracked from IANA data.

dst.note: Colombia does not observe DST.

geography.description: Colombia across the northern Andes and Caribbean coast, using a single UTC−5 time nationwide.

history.note: Colombia adopted UTC−5 as national standard time in the early 20th century and has not used modern recurring DST.

dst.note: Gulf Standard Time does not observe DST.

geography.description: The southeastern Arabian Peninsula around the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, anchored by the UAE and Oman.

history.note: Gulf states standardized around UTC+4 through the 20th century as regional administration and aviation networks modernized.
